extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers interested in political history, statesmanship, and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the character, capacities, and failings of a constitutional (cabinet) statesman — especially qualities that make an effective administrator or lead to apparent inconsistency. Focuses on traits illustrated by Sir Robert Peel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative competence / managerial ability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prime Minister (or chief minister) must master the practical business of government: read every important despatch, be cognisant of current correspondence in departments (e.g., India, Foreign Affairs, Ireland), conduct patronage inquiries, reply to persons of station, receive deputations, and attend Parliament long hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote: 'You must presume that he reads every important despatch... how can the Prime Minister be able to judge of the course of policy with regard to India, unless he be cognisant of all the current important correspondence?' Examples: writing replies with his own hand; attending six or seven hours a day during Parliament. The passage emphasizes day-to-day managerial tasks as central to the office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for industry and continuous application
rubrics_metrics.description: A great administrator must possess steady, regular industry and the capacity for sustained application rather than sporadic flashes of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with Byron: Peel's mind 'resembled the daily accumulating insensible deposits of a rich alluvial soil.' Such continuous application enables handling the 'enormous pressure of daily-growing business' which aristocratic leisure cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receptivity and sympathy with public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitutional statesman must sympathise with the ideas of the many and be able to change with public sentiment rather than remain hermetically sealed in original opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states: 'A constitutional statesman must sympathise in the ideas of the many. As the many change, it will be his good fortune if he can contrive to change with them.' Being receptive is a political necessity under popular government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical-mindedness / applying business notions to government
rubrics_metrics.description: The new industrial/middle-class representative wishes government to be administered according to the plain-sense notions familiar in business life rather than mysterious abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: 'They wished to see plain sense applied to the most prominent part of practical life.' This quality shapes policy orientation and priorities for administrators representing commercial interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance of collective responsibility / willingness to subordinate private opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabinet ministers are expected, in many cases, to support measures they privately opposed in cabinet in order to maintain government unity and effective administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peel's quotation defends the practice: ministers may 'give up that private opinion out of deference to his party' and still support collective measures; the passage explains secrecy and co-operation within cabinet and why insisting on literal consistency would make government impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to perform under routine and distraction (resisting intellectual benumbing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A minister must be able to sustain judgment and form sound convictions despite the benumbing effects of routine, continuous detail, and distracting transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that 'the most benumbing thing to the intellect is routine; the most bewildering is distraction' and gives the ledger analogy: chained to constant accounting, one cannot expect sound convictions on large issues. The criterion is about maintaining mental clarity amid administrative tedium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement about immediate detail versus long-term foresight
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrator's natural focus on immediate, pressing details can limit long-range speculation; a good statesman must nonetheless possess some overarching plan (even if not wholly original).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: administrators concentrate on 'the details of the day' and are 'unforseeing' by temperament; yet 'a man cannot conduct the detail of affairs without having some plan which regulates that detail' — the plan is often inherited or adopted rather than invented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangerous habit of advocacy / debating skill vs. conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill as a debater can separate the faculty of argument from the capacity of belief, leading ministers to defend positions they do not genuinely hold and to impair deep reasoning and original thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macaulay (quoted) and the essay note that parliamentary debating trains minds to produce 'arguments such as no man of sense would ever put into a treatise' and that 'they are obliged... to employ arguments which they do not think conclusive' — this habit tends to corrupt intellectual honesty and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative training and technical acquaintance with official forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical apprenticeship and experience in office (training in official forms and procedures) are valuable; being 'a man of business' in administrative technique is a strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Peel's apprenticeship to Mr. Percival supplied the technical acquaintance that made him an effective 'agent' rather than a great thinker; the Whigs' long absence from office left them 'not men of business' initially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to manage the complexity of a free government
rubrics_metrics.description: Under liberal/free government, the scale and complexity of supervision increases dramatically; a statesman must handle many varied, interlacing relations and unpredictable effects of change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: contrasted with despotic government, free governments must 'regulate one per cent of a hundred men's actions' rather than 'ten percent of ten' — the passage stresses the enlarged scope and uncertainty administrators must cope with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency vs. pragmatic priority-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: A statesman will often concede secondary issues to secure victory on primary ones; later, when priorities shift, what appears as a change of opinion may be pragmatic reassertion rather than genuine inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: conceding X to secure A or B when A,B are pressing; when X later becomes central, the statesman cannot easily demonstrate he never really changed opinion because of cabinet secrecy and changing public priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptiveness to social origins and constituency language
rubrics_metrics.description: A statesman's social origin and background shape his language and sympathies; those risen from the middle classes will naturally express and represent middle-class habits and notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay observes that middle-class men 'unmistakably speaking its language, inevitably thinking its thoughts' — this is not a defect but explains political positioning and the appeals a statesman makes.
